parsed.study_design: Mixed-methods case study using document review, structured questionnaires, and in-depth key-informant interviews
parsed.population_and_sample: Rural water-supply stakeholders and water-point institutions in Ohangwena Region; interviews included Directorate of Rural Water Supply personnel and chairpersons of Local Water User Associations and Water Point Committees (the reported category counts are internally inconsistent with the stated total of nine informants).
parsed.exposure: Community-based and decentralized management of rural water points, including legal-framework implementation, role delineation, committee governance, community participation, training, incentives, and government post-construction support.
parsed.outcome: Functionality and sustainability of rural water points and associated access to potable water, including breakdown or abandonment of water points, affordability-related nonpayment, and service quantity and quality concerns.
parsed.rationale: The Methodology section (pp. 32–34) identifies a mixed-methods case study using policy and document review plus primary interviews with officials and community water-management representatives. The Findings and Discussion section (pp. 34–36) empirically links legal uncertainty, weak committee governance, limited participation and training, variable pricing, and inadequate post-construction support to water-point dysfunction, abandonment, nonpayment, and reduced potable-water access. This directly addresses governance and administrative determinants of rural household and community water-service availability and sustainability.
